html:
The Mayo, who call themselves Yoreme, are an Indigenous people of southern Sonora and northern Sinaloa in Mexico, along the Mayo and Fuerte rivers. They speak a Cáhita language close to that of the Yaqui.

In 1492 they lived in farming villages on the river floodplains. Unlike the Yaqui, they invited the Jesuits in, and missions were founded among them from 1614. They joined the Yaqui in a great revolt in 1740. In the 1800s Mexican governments took their land for haciendas, and they rose again in the 1870s and 1880s; their lands were later turned into large irrigated farms. The Yoreme keep a mix of Catholic and older ritual, including the deer dance and the Easter ceremonies of the fariseos. Some 40,000 people speak Mayo today.
